### Genocide and Conquest: The Definition, the Intent Test, and Where the Courts Drew the Line

Filed as: Special Report No. 7 — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-08T20:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-08-genocide-and-conquest.html

Special Report

 The Definition File — Coinage, Convention, and the Courts

 Objective

 Genocide and Conquest: The Definition, the Intent Test, and Where the Courts Drew the Line

 “Genocide” is a word with a birth certificate: coined in print in 1944, defined by treaty in 1948 as five acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, in whole or in part, as such, and applied by courts only where that intent is proven to the standard the International Court of Justice set—the only reasonable inference from the record. “Conquest” is the older word: it names the transfer of peoples and territory by force, and it carries no legal test at all. The desk files the coinage, the Convention, the older record the word was carried back to, and the judgments, in that order.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 2000 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026.

The File in Brief

The word is younger than the practice it names, and the record keeps the two apart. Raphael Lemkin, a Polish jurist, coined “genocide” in his 1944 book Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, joining the Greek genos (race, tribe) to the Latin -cide (killing), and defined it as “the destruction of a nation or of an ethnic group”—a coordinated plan against the essential foundations of a group’s life, of which mass killing is one instrument among several. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on December 9, 1948; it entered into force on January 12, 1951. Article I declares the crime punishable “whether committed in time of peace or in time of war.” Article II lists five acts—killing, serious bodily or mental harm, conditions of life calculated to destroy, measures to prevent births, forcible transfer of children—and attaches all five to a single mental element: intent to destroy the group, in whole or in part, as such. The courts call that element dolus specialis, specific intent, and the International Court of Justice ruled in 2015 that it is “the essential characteristic of genocide, which distinguishes it from other crimes.” On that test the adjudicated record is narrow. The Rwanda tribunal’s 1998 judgment in Akayesu was the first genocide conviction by an international court. The Cambodia tribunal convicted the Khmer Rouge leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan of genocide in 2018, for the Vietnamese and, in Nuon Chea’s case, the Cham. The International Court of Justice in 2007 found that the July 1995 killings at Srebrenica—more than 7,000 Bosniak men and boys—were genocide, and found Serbia in breach of its duty to prevent them; the same judgment declined to find genocide across the wider Bosnian war. In 2015 the Court dismissed both Croatia’s claim against Serbia and Serbia’s counter-claim, holding in each direction that the material acts were established and the specific intent was unproven: the campaigns aimed at forced displacement, the record’s word, and displacement stands outside the Article II list. Executive governments apply the word on a different instrument: the United States has issued eight formal genocide determinations since 1993, the eighth being Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s March 21, 2022 determination on the Rohingya, and President Joseph Biden’s April 12, 2022 statement calling Russia’s war in Ukraine genocide was a presidential characterization that no formal determination followed. The word’s spread through print is measurable: Google Books data assembled by the historian Dominik Schaller show decided rises in the second half of the 1960s and in the 1990s, and “genocide” has appeared in books more often than “massacre” since the late 1990s. The older record, the centuries of conquest the word now gets carried back to, was written in a different vocabulary: Thucydides records Athens killing the men of military age it captured on Melos in 416 BC, enslaving the women and children, and settling 500 colonists on the island, and no word in his account corresponds to the 1944 coinage. The desk files the coinage and the Convention first, the older record second, the retrospective application third, and the courts’ line last, closing in a four-column ledger.

1. The Coinage: A Word With a Birth Certificate

Raphael Lemkin put the word into print in November 1944. Axis Rule in Occupied Europe: Laws of Occupation, Analysis of Government, Proposals for Redress, published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, is a compilation of the occupation law of Axis Europe, and its ninth chapter, titled “Genocide,” opens with the coinage: “New conceptions require new terms. By ‘genocide’ we mean the destruction of a nation or of an ethnic group. This new word, coined by the author to denote an old practice in its modern development, is made from the ancient Greek word genos (race, tribe) and the Latin cide (killing), thus corresponding in its formation to such words as tyrannicide, homicide, infanticide, etc.” Lemkin’s own biography sits inside the book’s occasion: he was a Polish lawyer of Jewish descent who had fled Poland in 1939, and 49 members of his family were killed in the Holocaust.

Lemkin’s definition ran wider than killing, and he said so in the same passage. “Generally speaking, genocide does not necessarily mean the immediate destruction of a nation, except when accomplished by mass killings of all members of a nation. It is intended rather to signify a coordinated plan of different actions aiming at the destruction of essential foundations of the life of national groups, with the aim of annihilating the groups themselves.” The chapter then works through the fields in which such a plan operates—political, social, cultural, economic, biological, physical, religious, and moral—and states the aim in terms of substitution as well as destruction: the oppressor’s own national pattern imposed on the emptied ground. The object of the crime, in Lemkin’s construction, is the group as an entity; the acts fall on individuals as members of the group.

The word entered a courtroom document within a year, as description rather than as charge. The indictment of the major German war criminals at Nuremberg, filed October 18, 1945, charges under Count Three, war crimes, that the defendants “conducted deliberate and systematic genocide, viz., the extermination of racial and national groups, against the civilian populations of certain occupied territories in order to destroy particular races and classes of people and national, racial or religious groups, particularly Jews, Poles and Gypsies and others.” The Charter of the International Military Tribunal, the instrument that defined the tribunal’s charges, contains no such word; genocide appears in the indictment as a term for conduct charged under the existing counts. On December 11, 1946, the General Assembly’s Resolution 96 (I) affirmed genocide as a crime under international law, and the drafting of a convention followed. The sequence is the file’s spine: a scholar’s coinage in 1944, a prosecutor’s descriptive use in 1945, an Assembly affirmation in 1946, a treaty definition in 1948.

2. The Convention: Five Acts, Four Groups, One Intent

The treaty text is short, and its architecture is exact. Article I: “The Contracting Parties confirm that genocide, whether committed in time of peace or in time of war, is a crime under international law which they undertake to prevent and to punish.” Article II defines the crime as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”: (a) killing members of the group; (b) causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; (c) deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; (d) imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; (e) forcibly transferring children of the group to another group. Article III makes punishable the crime itself and, beside it, conspiracy to commit genocide, direct and public incitement, attempt, and complicity. The Convention’s preamble records that “at all periods of history genocide has inflicted great losses on humanity”—the treaty’s own acknowledgment that the practice predates the word. Article IX sends disputes between states over the Convention’s interpretation and application to the International Court of Justice, the door through which every state-versus-state case in this file arrived.

Four features of the definition govern everything the courts have done with it. First, the protected list is closed: national, ethnical, racial, and religious groups. Political groups stand outside it; the destruction of a political class, however complete, is charged under other law. Second, three of the five acts involve no killing: serious mental harm, birth prevention, and child transfer can each complete the crime. Third, the acts carry the crime only when joined to the intent to destroy the group as such; the same killing, committed with the intent to expel, to punish, or to win ground, is a different offense in the Convention’s scheme. Fourth, Article I severs the crime from war in the treaty’s first sentence: the crime exists in peacetime on the same terms as in wartime, and war crimes law, which attaches to armed conflict, has no corresponding clause. The Convention entered into force on January 12, 1951, ninety days after the twentieth ratification, and its definition was carried nearly verbatim into the statutes of the Rwanda and Yugoslavia tribunals, the Cambodia chambers, and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court.

The intent element is where cases are won and lost, and the courts have priced it high. In its judgment of February 3, 2015, in Croatia v. Serbia, the International Court of Justice stated the doctrine at paragraph 132: the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such” is “the essential characteristic of genocide, which distinguishes it from other crimes,” a dolus specialis, a specific intent, which must be present in addition to the intent required for each individual act. Where intent is to be inferred from a pattern of conduct, the Court’s standing test, applied in both the 2007 and 2015 judgments, requires that the genocidal intent be the only reasonable inference the pattern supports. Discriminatory intent—targeting members of a group for abuse, expulsion, or killing as enemies—does not by itself satisfy the test; the inference must run to destruction of the group, in whole or in part, as an end. Every judgment in section 6 of this report turns on that paragraph and that test.

3. The Older Record: Conquest Before the Word

The ancient record describes the outcomes in the vocabulary of war and victory, and the outcomes themselves need no translation. Thucydides, in Book V of his History of the Peloponnesian War, records the Athenian expedition against the island of Melos in 416 BC: a neutral Dorian island that refused submission to the Athenian alliance. His account gives the negotiation as the Melian Dialogue, in which the Athenian envoys state the operating rule in the open—right is in question between equals in power; the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must—and then gives the result in one sentence: the Melians surrendered at discretion, the Athenians put to death all the grown men they had taken, sold the women and children for slaves, and sent out 500 colonists to settle the place themselves. The passage is the classical world’s own description of a conquest that ended a people’s civic existence on its island. Thucydides files it as war.

Carthage supplies the largest ancient specimen, and its numbers come with their instruments attached. The Yale historian Ben Kiernan’s study “The First Genocide: Carthage, 146 BC,” published in Diogenes in 2004, assembles the ancient accounts: Cato the Censor’s standing close to his Senate speeches from 153 BC, Delenda est Carthago—Carthage must be destroyed—which Kiernan identifies as possibly the first recorded incitement to genocide; the three-year siege; a population he puts at 200,000 to 400,000, of whom at least 150,000 perished; and the end in 146 BC, when Scipio Aemilianus razed the city and dispersed the 55,000 survivors, including 25,000 women, into slavery. Kiernan also records the limits of the file: the famous salting of the earth appears in no ancient source, and the earliest claim of it he traces dates to 1930. The ancient writers themselves—Polybius, an eyewitness attached to Scipio’s staff, and Appian, writing three centuries later—describe destruction, extermination of the city’s population in the fighting, and enslavement of the remnant, in the vocabulary available to them. The word applied to the event in Kiernan’s title dates from 1944.

Lemkin himself drew the line of descent, in a footnote. Chapter nine of Axis Rule cites, as classical examples of wars of extermination in which nations and groups were completely or almost completely destroyed, the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC and of Jerusalem by Titus, the religious wars of Islam and the Crusades, the massacres of the Albigenses and the Waldenses, and the siege of Magdeburg in the Thirty Years’ War, and adds the wholesale massacres in the wars of Genghis Khan and Tamerlane. His unfinished History of Genocide, planned in three volumes and left in manuscript at his death in 1959, assigned nine chapters to antiquity—among them Assyria, Carthage, Gaul, and the Celts—twelve to the Middle Ages, among them the Albigensians, the Mongols, the Moors, and medieval England, and forty-one to modern times. The retrospective application of the word, documented in section 4, begins with the word’s own inventor, and it begins as history rather than as law: Lemkin’s chapters judge the dead by a definition written in 1944, and no court has ever been asked to do the same, the Convention having no retroactive reach.

4. The Word Carried Backward: Retrospective Application

The scholarly application of “genocide” to conquests widened in steps, and the steps are datable. The word’s frequency in print, measured in the Google Books corpus of more than five million books and assembled by Dominik Schaller in Genocide Studies and Prevention in 2011, shows no single explosion: decided rises came in the second half of the 1960s—Schaller and the literature after him associate the rise with the fiftieth anniversary of the Armenian genocide in 1965, with the violence of post-independence Rwanda and Burundi, and with the Vietnam War and the American civil-rights movement—and again in the 1990s, with the field of genocide studies expanding rapidly after the Cold War’s end. Since the late 1990s the corpus has used “genocide” more often than “massacre.” The retrospective shelf grew with the frequency: David E. Stannard’s American Holocaust: Columbus and the Conquest of the New World (Oxford University Press, 1992) argued that within twenty-one years of Columbus’s first landing the island he renamed Hispaniola was effectively desolate, nearly 8,000,000 people killed, in Stannard’s accounting, by violence, disease, and despair; that historical demographers had found post-contact depopulation rates of 90 to 98 percent region by region, with an overall decline of about 95 percent as a working rule of thumb; and that the destruction of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas was “far and away, the most massive act of genocide in the history of the world.” The desk files Stannard’s numbers as his: the pre-contact population of Hispaniola is contested across a wide range in the demographic literature, and Stannard’s figures stand at the high end of it, a placement his appendix argues for directly.

States have also applied the word backward, and the instruments they use record the strain of doing so. In May 2021, after negotiations begun in 2015, Germany and Namibia initialled a joint declaration on the German colonial war of 1904 to 1908 in what is now Namibia, in which General Lothar von Trotha’s extermination order of October 2, 1904 stands at the head of a campaign in which, on the standard estimates, about 65,000 Herero—about 80 percent of the people—and about 10,000 Nama—about 50 percent—perished by killing, starvation, and the camps. The declaration’s operative sentence is written in the present tense looking back: the atrocities “culminated in events that, from today’s perspective, would be called genocide.” Germany coupled the acknowledgment to &euro;1.1 billion over thirty years for reconstruction and development programs, and both governments framed the money as reconciliation; the declaration carries no legal duty of reparations, Germany’s stated ground being that the prohibition of genocide in international law postdates 1904 to 1908. Descendant organizations of the Herero and Nama rejected the declaration, on the record, for negotiating over their heads and for the exclusion of reparations. In the same year, 2021, the United States recognized the Armenian genocide of 1915 to 1916, a determination that arrived a century after the events and against the background of the Ottoman Empire’s wartime deportations and massacres. In each case the naming instrument is political—a declaration, a presidential statement—and in each case the namer states, or the record shows, that the legal category postdates the events it is carried back to.

5. Genocide Without War: The Crime Detached From Battle

Article I’s clause—in time of peace or in time of war—has a case record, and Cambodia is its center. On November 16, 2018, the Trial Chamber of the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicted Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan, the two surviving senior leaders of Democratic Kampuchea, of genocide, and sentenced both to life imprisonment, for crimes committed between April 17, 1975 and January 6, 1979. Both men were convicted of genocide against the Vietnamese ethnic, national, and racial group; Nuon Chea was convicted in addition of genocide against the Cham ethnic and religious group, on the basis of his superior responsibility. The convictions arose from a state’s campaign against groups inside its own territory and under its own administration—minorities marked out within a population the regime already ruled—and the same judgment’s structure displays the Convention’s boundary from the other side: the far larger killing of ethnic Khmers by the Khmer Rouge, the regime’s own national group destroyed in the hundreds of thousands as class and political enemies, was prosecuted in the case as crimes against humanity, because Article II’s closed list covers national, ethnical, racial, and religious groups and the Khmer victims were targeted as political and social categories. The largest part of one of the century’s largest killings stands outside the genocide counts of its own tribunal, on the text of the definition.

The first conviction under the Convention carries the same lesson in miniature. On September 2, 1998, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda convicted Jean-Paul Akayesu, the bourgmestre of Taba commune, on nine of fifteen counts, including genocide and direct and public incitement to commit genocide, and sentenced him to life imprisonment—the first genocide conviction by an international tribunal, fifty years after the Convention’s adoption. The judgment also held, for the first time in an international court, that rape and sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide when committed with the specific intent, under the Article II head of causing serious bodily or mental harm. The Rwanda killings of 1994 ran alongside a civil war, and the tribunal’s statute covered both; the genocide counts in the judgment attach to intent and to the protected group, and the war supplies setting rather than element. Article III completes the detachment: conspiracy and direct and public incitement are punishable as such, so the crime in law can be complete before any of the five acts occurs, in a radio studio as readily as on a battlefield.

6. War Without the Finding: The Intent Test Applied

The Bosnian case is the fullest worked example of a war passing through the test and emerging divided. Bosnia and Herzegovina sued Serbia and Montenegro under Article IX in 1993, alleging a campaign of genocide across the war of 1992 to 1995. In its judgment of February 26, 2007, the International Court of Justice concluded that the acts committed at Srebrenica in July 1995—the killing of more than 7,000 Bosniak men and boys by forces of the Republika Srpska—fell within Article II (a) and (b) and were committed with the specific intent to destroy in part the group of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina as such, and were accordingly acts of genocide. The Court found that Serbia had neither committed that genocide nor been complicit in it, and it found Serbia in breach of the Article I obligation to prevent it, and of its obligations to cooperate with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including by failing to transfer Ratko Mladić. The wider campaign—killings, detention camps, and mass expulsion across Bosnia, documented in the same record—produced no genocide finding. One enclave in eleven days met the test; a three-year war around it did not, and the difference the Court recorded is the presence, at Srebrenica, of an intent it could name.

The Croatia case ran the instrument in both directions and it returned the same reading twice. Croatia claimed Serbia was responsible for genocide in the war of 1991 to 1995; Serbia counter-claimed over Operation Storm of August 1995, in which more than 200,000 Serbs fled or were expelled from the Krajina. On February 3, 2015, the Court rejected Croatia’s claim by fifteen votes to two and Serbia’s counter-claim unanimously, in a single judgment. For each claim the Court found the actus reus established—killings and serious harm within Article II’s list, committed by the other side’s forces—and the dolus specialis unproven: the conduct, on the evidence, aimed at the forced displacement of the population from territory, and displacement, however violent, is an aim the Convention’s list does not convert into destruction of the group. The judgment is the standing citation for the gap this report files: a war can satisfy the physical half of the definition at scale, on both sides, and satisfy the mental half on neither.

Darfur shows the same events passing through two different instruments and returning two different answers, six years apart. The United States ran its own instrument first: a State Department team interviewed 1,136 Darfurian refugees at nineteen locations in eastern Chad between July 12 and August 18, 2004, of whom 74 percent reported Sudanese military involvement in the attacks on their villages, and on September 9, 2004 Secretary of State Colin Powell told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that “genocide has been committed in Darfur and the Government of Sudan and the jinjaweed bear responsibility—and genocide may still be occurring”—the first invocation of the Convention by a sitting United States official for an ongoing crisis. The International Criminal Court’s instrument ran slower and under judicial standards: its first warrant for President Omar Al Bashir, March 4, 2009, charged war crimes and crimes against humanity and carried no genocide count, the Pre-Trial Chamber’s majority holding the genocidal intent not then established to its standard; after the Appeals Chamber ruled that standard too demanding for the warrant stage, a second warrant issued on July 12, 2010, adding three counts of genocide—by killing, by causing serious bodily or mental harm, and by deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy—against the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa groups, on reasonable grounds to believe Al Bashir acted with the specific intent. Al Bashir was never surrendered to the Court and never tried. The executive determination of 2004 and the judicial warrant of 2010 name the same crime over the same ground; the six years between them are the distance between the two instruments’ standards of proof.

7. The Word in Present Wars: Determinations, Characterizations, and Provisional Measures

Governments now apply the word through a standing administrative practice, and the practice has a ledger. Secretary Blinken’s statement of March 21, 2022, at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, announcing his determination that members of the Burmese military committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya, counted the practice aloud: “Beyond the Holocaust, the United States has concluded that genocide was committed seven times. Today marks the eighth.” The seven, in the order the United States recognized them, were Bosnia, Rwanda, Iraq, Darfur, the territories ISIS held and the Yazidis it targeted, China and the Uyghurs, and Armenia. A determination is an executive act: it carries political and statutory consequences inside the issuing government and binds no court. Beside the ledger stands the looser instrument of characterization. On April 12, 2022, in Iowa, President Biden said of Russia’s war in Ukraine, “Yes, I called it genocide,” adding that it had become clearer that President Putin was “just trying to wipe out the idea of even being able to be Ukrainian,” and in the same exchange assigned the legal question elsewhere: “We’ll let the lawyers decide internationally whether or not it qualifies, but it sure seems that way to me.” No formal State Department genocide determination on Ukraine followed; the Department’s formal accusation of March 23, 2022 charged war crimes. Other governments divided on the word in public: President Emmanuel Macron of France declined to adopt it for Ukraine, describing Russian actions as war crimes. Russia’s own stated ground for its invasion included the claim that Ukraine was committing genocide in the Donbas, and Ukraine carried that claim to the International Court of Justice as the applicant: in its judgment on preliminary objections of February 2, 2024, the Court found jurisdiction to entertain Ukraine’s request for a declaration that there is no credible evidence Ukraine committed genocide in the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, and found it lacked jurisdiction over Ukraine’s submissions on Russia’s use of force; by an order of December 5, 2025, the Court found Russia’s counter-claims in the case admissible, with pleadings now running into 2027. The word in that file has been claim, counter-claim, and stated cause of war, and the Court has so far ruled on which questions it may hear.

At the Court, the live genocide cases stand at the provisional stage, and the provisional stage has a precise meaning that the record states in its own terms. In The Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court’s unanimous order of January 23, 2020 found the rights The Gambia claimed for the Rohingya plausible, found a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to them, and ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent acts within Article II; the order decided nothing on the merits, which remain pending. In South Africa v. Israel, filed December 29, 2023, South Africa alleges that Israel’s campaign in Gaza breaches the Convention; Israel’s stated position, presented at the January 2024 hearings, is that the case presents a grossly distorted picture, that Israel is fighting Hamas in self-defense after the October 7, 2023 attack, and that the intent element of genocide is, in its counsel’s words, completely missing. The Court’s order of January 26, 2024 found at least some of the rights South Africa claimed plausible—including the right of Palestinians in Gaza to be protected from acts of genocide—and indicated provisional measures; further orders of March 28 and May 24, 2024, the last by thirteen votes to two, ordered Israel immediately to halt its military offensive in the Rafah Governorate and any other action there risking conditions of life capable of bringing about the group’s physical destruction in whole or in part. The Court has issued no finding that genocide occurred; its then-president, Judge Joan Donoghue, stated publicly in April 2024 that the Court decided the Palestinians had a plausible right to protection and did not decide that the claim of genocide was plausible. A separate United Nations body, the Human Rights Council’s Commission of Inquiry, concluded in September 2025 that genocide had been committed in Gaza, finding four of the five Article II acts and intent as the only reasonable inference; Israel rejects the Commission’s findings, and the Commission is an investigative body whose conclusions bind no court. Written pleadings in the Court case run to 2029. The desk files the three instruments at their own grades: a court’s provisional measures, which protect rights pending judgment; an inquiry’s conclusions, which persuade or fail to; and a merits judgment, which does not yet exist in the case.

8. The Two Categories, as the Record Defines Them

War and genocide, in the instruments this file has used, are defined on different axes, and the adjudicated record shows the overlap and the remainder on both sides. The laws of war attach to armed conflict: the Geneva Conventions of 1949 govern international and non-international armed conflict, and a war crime in the tribunal statutes requires conduct linked to such a conflict. The category is defined by the parties and the fighting. Genocide is defined by a target and an intent: a protected group, and the purpose of destroying it in whole or in part. Scale appears in neither definition as a threshold. The genocide finding of the modern record rests on eleven days and more than 7,000 victims at Srebrenica, because the intent was proven; the expulsion of more than 200,000 people in Operation Storm drew no such finding, because it was not. Of the three tribunal matters that have produced genocide convictions—Rwanda in 1998, Srebrenica in the Yugoslavia tribunal’s judgments, and Cambodia in 2018—two arose inside wars and one inside a regime’s administration of its own state. The executive ledger and the press usage run wider than the judicial record in every period the file covers, and the distance between the word as governments and newspapers use it and the word as courts apply it is the quantity the cases measure: identical in spelling, different in standard, and separated, in the instances documented here, by the single element of proven intent to destroy a group as such. The older word, conquest, belongs to neither axis: no treaty defines it, no court applies it, and its record—Melos emptied and recolonized, Carthage razed and its survivors enslaved, peoples transferred and territories annexed across the centuries the word governed—was written by its makers as victory and by its subjects as catastrophe, in vocabularies that predate the legal one by two thousand years and more.

9. The Ledger

The whole subject, sorted by the state of its evidence. The desk closes the file with the four-column accounting the report has applied throughout, to every side’s claims at the same grade. Verified: established by treaty text, adjudication, or the official record. Documented-but-small: real, proven, and bounded by its instrument. Claimed-but-unproven: asserted by named makers, awaiting or lacking adjudication. Disproven: tested by the instrument built to test it and failed.

VerifiedDocumented-but-smallClaimed-but-unprovenDisproven

“Genocide” was coined by Raphael Lemkin in Axis Rule in Occupied Europe (1944), from genos and -cide, defined as the destruction of a nation or ethnic group by a coordinated plan against the foundations of its life. The word’s first courtroom appearance is descriptive, in Count Three of the Nuremberg indictment (1945); the Charter contains no such charge. The Convention (adopted December 9, 1948; in force January 12, 1951) defines the crime as five acts against a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, committed with intent to destroy it in whole or in part, as such, “in time of peace or in time of war.” Specific intent (dolus specialis) is “the essential characteristic of genocide” (ICJ, 2015, para. 132). Adjudicated: Akayesu (ICTR, 1998), the first international genocide conviction, rape held an act of genocide; Srebrenica a genocide (ICJ, 2007), Serbia in breach of the duty to prevent; the Cambodia convictions of 2018 (Vietnamese; Cham, Nuon Chea). The United States has made eight formal determinations, the Rohingya last (March 21, 2022). Thucydides records Melos: men of military age killed, women and children enslaved, 500 colonists settled (416 BC).
The adjudicated set is small against the word’s usage: three tribunal matters have produced genocide convictions (Rwanda, the Yugoslavia cases over Srebrenica, Cambodia), and the International Court of Justice has found genocide established in one place, Srebrenica, across three state-versus-state judgments. Kiernan’s Carthage file is bounded by its sources: a population of 200,000 to 400,000, at least 150,000 dead, 55,000 enslaved—estimates built on Polybius and Appian. Germany’s Namibia acknowledgment is bounded by its own text: the word applied “from today’s perspective,” &euro;1.1 billion as reconciliation, no legal reparations duty accepted. The United States’ Darfur determination rested on 1,136 refugee interviews in Chad.
President Biden’s April 12, 2022 characterization of Russia’s war in Ukraine as genocide: a presidential statement, expressly left by its maker to “the lawyers,” with no formal determination following. Russia’s claim that Ukraine committed genocide in the Donbas, the stated ground of invasion: before the International Court of Justice as a request for a declaration that no credible evidence supports it, counter-claims admitted December 2025, undecided. South Africa’s allegation of genocide in Gaza: provisional measures granted on plausible rights, merits undecided, pleadings to 2029; the UN Commission of Inquiry’s September 2025 conclusion of genocide is an investigative finding, rejected by Israel, binding no court. Stannard’s Hispaniola figures—nearly 8,000,000 dead, 95 percent decline—are one historian’s high-end accounting in a contested demographic field.
The claim that the International Court of Justice found genocide, or a plausible claim of genocide, in Gaza: the Court’s January 2024 order found claimed rights plausible and its then-president stated on the record that it did not decide the claim of genocide was plausible; no merits finding exists. The claim that mass expulsion satisfies the Convention: tested in Croatia v. Serbia (2015) with the acts established on both sides, and failed on intent in both directions. The salting of Carthage’s earth: no ancient source records it; the earliest trace Kiernan found dates to 1930. The claim that genocide requires a war: Article I’s text and the Cambodia convictions stand against it. The claim that the Nuremberg Charter charged genocide: the word appears in the indictment’s description under Count Three and in no article of the Charter.

The file, closed, reads as follows. A word coined in 1944 for an old practice acquired, in 1948, a definition with four protected groups, five acts, and one intent; the courts that apply the definition have sustained it in a handful of matters and refused it in wars whose violence is not in dispute; governments apply the word by determination and characterization at lower standards and on faster clocks; and the centuries of conquest that precede the word sit in the record under their own vocabulary, carried into the modern one by historians and declarations that state, in their own texts, that the category postdates the events. The distinction the instruments draw is consistent across all of it: war is measured by its parties and its conduct, genocide by its target and its proven intent, and the two measures return different answers on the same ground often enough that the cases, rather than the vocabulary, are where the line is kept.

 The File, Clipped

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty items.

 

 SubjectiveRaphael Lemkin — Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, chapter IX, “Genocide” (Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 1944)The coinage itself: the definition, the etymology, the eight fields of the coordinated plan, and the footnote carrying the classical line of descent—Carthage, Jerusalem, the Albigenses and Waldenses, Magdeburg, Genghis Khan and Tamerlane. The primary text beneath sections 1 and 3.

 SubjectiveConvention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide — adopted December 9, 1948, in force January 12, 1951 (United Nations Treaty Series No. 1021)The treaty text: Article I’s peace-or-war clause, Article II’s five acts and closed list of groups, Article III’s punishable acts, Article IX’s road to The Hague. Every legal statement in the report is a reading of this document.

 SubjectiveIndictment of the Major War Criminals, Count Three — International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg, filed October 18, 1945 (Avalon Project transcript)The word’s first courtroom appearance: “deliberate and systematic genocide, viz., the extermination of racial and national groups,” charged as description under the war-crimes count. The Charter beside it contains no such word.

 SubjectiveThucydides — History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V, chapters 84–116 (the Melian Dialogue and the fall of Melos, 416 BC)The classical record in its own vocabulary: the envoys’ rule of power, the surrender at discretion, the men killed, the women and children sold, the 500 colonists. The desk’s specimen of the older record, written by the conquering side’s own historian.

### Seven Dead on the Railway at Al-Ayyat, the Six of the Square Are Named in Kraków, and Eisenkot Sets His Four Conditions in Jerusalem

Filed as: Edition No. 22 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-08T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Seven Dead on the Railway at Al-Ayyat, the Six of the Square Are Named in Kraków, and Eisenkot Sets His Four Conditions in Jerusalem

 The day’s developments whole, at the evening hour: a railway collision south of Cairo supplied the day’s new dead, its toll rising in steps all afternoon; Kraków’s mourning acquired names and ages for its six, a spokesman’s “highly likely” joining the square to the house in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and a political challenge to the minister who read the attack aloud on Saturday; a drone fell on rescue crews working the worst single bombing of Ukraine’s week; the Gulf file added projectile impacts reported on Qeshm, projectiles reported fired from Sirik, and a gas field halted by a drone in Iraqi Kurdistan; Jerusalem’s mandate-holder published his four conditions and met no coalition; Asunción’s case widened to at least twenty-seven charged while the repayments to savers reached $160 million; and the American count, the quake count apart, ended the day exactly where Friday left it.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 21, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today. Where the evening figures differ from the midday’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The midday edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

Sunday evening is a file of tolls revised upward, names supplied, and positions stated for the record, and the desk files it in that order. In Egypt, a train running from Giza to Fayoum struck the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan train standing in the Al-Ayyat district, and the Health Ministry’s count climbed through the day—four dead and 88 injured in the first official figures, seven dead and 112 injured in the ministry’s later count, with one account carrying 125 injured—in the ministry’s figures as reported through the day filed below. In Kraków, officials identified the six killed in the Main Market Square by age and nationality, prosecutors’ spokesman Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the same person carried out the killings in the square and at the suspect’s home, and the square itself reopened late Sunday, in Reuters’ evening account filed below. In Ukraine, a Russian drone struck the rescue crews at Komyshuvakha, where Monday’s bombing of a former school and a shelter killed at least 55 people and about 50 remain missing. In the Gulf, Iranian media reported projectile impacts on Qeshm Island late Sunday and Iranian state television reported three projectiles launched from Sirik toward vessels; in Iraqi Kurdistan a drone attack halted production at the Khor Mor gas field, in the live file filed below. In Jerusalem, Mr. Eisenkot, mandate in hand, set four conditions for joining his government and challenged the parties that called for unity to form it under him; no faction accepted on Sunday, and no coalition exists. In Asunción, the Ueno case widened—at least 27 people face charges, and the central bank has paid $160 million to nearly 1.2 million savers. In the United States the Senate count did not move at all: Mississippi stands at 2,574 votes on a tally stamped Friday, Alaska at 637, and both wait on Tuesday. That is the evening whole: one new disaster counted, one case named, one mandate conditioned, and a week whose every open question still falls on the same two days, Monday’s handovers and Tuesday’s deadlines.

Al-Ayyat at 1800: Seven Dead on the Railway

The day’s new event happened on the railway south of Cairo, and its numbers are a staircase. Train No. 134, running from Giza to Fayoum, struck the rear of Train No. 2010, running from Cairo to Aswan, between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations in the Al-Ayyat district of Giza province, the National Authority for Egyptian Railways said; several carriages left the track and some overturned. The chief prosecutor’s office said its initial inspection found the Giza–Fayoum train had hit the last carriage of the Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track, and that a train conductor was among the dead, in the collated account filed below. The Health Ministry’s first count, carried by the wires at midday, was four dead and 88 injured. By the evening the ministry’s toll stood at seven dead and 112 injured, reported by Sky News and Al Jazeera; a further account of the ministry’s figures carries 125 injured, 132 cases received by hospitals in all, 71 of the injured discharged and 43 still in hospital—23 at Al-Ayyat, 13 at Al-Wasta and 7 at Atfih. Seventy-two ambulances took part in the evacuation. The two injured counts, 112 and 125, are both in the record under the ministry’s name and the desk prints both; the dead, at seven, agree in every later account. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered an investigation and, in his words, that anyone found to have been negligent be held accountable; the prosecutor general sent a team to examine the site, assess the damage and fix the exact toll; railway crews and cranes were dispatched to clear the line. No cause has been stated by any authority. Al-Ayyat carries a record in this file: a fire on a holiday train there in 2002 killed more than 370 people, the worst disaster on Egypt’s railways. The dead of Sunday have not been named.

Kraków at 1800: The Six Are Named by Age, and the Minister Is Challenged

The mourning acquired its particulars on Sunday. Officials counted the six killed in the Main Market Square as a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50, in the evening brief compiled from the Polish and German reporting filed below; five foreign nationals—from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia—are among the wounded, Reuters reported. The wounded count itself did not settle: 15 in some accounts, 16 in others, and Reuters’ evening wording counts 16 wounded in addition to those killed, including the two police officers and the suspected gunman, who remains in critical condition in hospital. The two officers were woken from drug-induced comas after surgery, the evening brief reports, on the same day the prosecutors announced they had regained consciousness. At the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, the three bodies had gunshot wounds and firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition were recovered from the property, prosecutors’ office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said; it was “highly likely,” he said, that the killings there and in Kraków were carried out by the same person, and the investigations are ongoing. Highly likely is the strongest joining word any official has used, and the desk prints it as a spokesman’s assessment, not a finding. The suspect has still not been questioned, and no charge has been laid.

The day’s considered response in Poland was an argument about the reading, conducted in the open. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said on Saturday that everything points to the attacker having held “very, very radical views” and being “fascinated by far-right ideologies.” The nationalist opposition questioned the grounds: Przemysław Czarnek, deputy head of PiS, wrote that if Mr. Kierwiński “has misinformed the public, he should face political consequences,” and demanded immediate explanations and access to the information the statements rested on. On Sunday the minister declined to retreat: “We are not passing judgement,” he told the broadcaster TVN24. “Always, there are initial hypotheses, information and evidence&hellip; These are things now being checked by the police and I will not elaborate. Nobody is walking anything back.” The desk files the exchange whole: a minister’s hypothesis, an opposition’s demand for its basis, and a refusal to withdraw it, with the investigation that alone can settle the question still running and the man who could answer it unable to speak. The city’s own acts closed the day: the square and its surrounding streets, closed since Saturday, reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St. Mary’s tower, suspended for twelve hours overnight, was, the news agency PAP reported, silenced for the first time since 1939; and police tightened security in Warsaw and other cities. National mourning runs through Monday. One figure in this file moved against the paper’s earlier record and the desk states it plainly: the ages of the three found at home are now given as a father of 52 and a mother of 51 in the evening brief, against 53 and 52 in the police statement quoted by Reuters, while the sister stands at 21 in both—and at 20 in the prosecutors’ account the midday edition filed. Three ages, three triangles; the desk chooses in none of them.

Komyshuvakha and Abu Dhabi: A Drone on the Rescuers, and a Table Still Growing

Ukraine’s Sunday entry is a second strike on the site of the week’s worst one. A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions at Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, hitting the former school and the nearby shelter that guided bombs had blasted on Monday as residents waited for humanitarian aid, in the Associated Press account filed below. No one was injured in Sunday’s strike, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged. The Monday attack’s toll now stands at at least 55 dead, and around 50 people are still listed as missing, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, said; many of the bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members involved in what it calls the “double tap” strike—the second blow aimed at the same place after the first—and Ukraine has routinely accused Russia of striking the same site in quick succession to target the crews who respond. On Saturday the community buried its dead from the first strike: a farewell ceremony in Zaporizhzhia for six police officers killed at Komyshuvakha, three of them near the former school, and three residents buried near one another where a memorial is planned. No Russian statement on either strike was taken in by the evening. The accounts of both attacks rest on Ukrainian officials and the Associated Press’s reporting from the region; no party that did not issue them has verified the toll.

Two days before the Abu Dhabi table sits, its shape and its claims both grew. France’s confirmation that Europeans will take part acquired its details in the afternoon accounts: Mr. Barrot said he would not personally be at the negotiating table and that Paris had not yet named its representative, in the Euronews account filed below; Russia’s delegation will be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, in the confirmation account filed below; and the G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday. The American president’s expectation is also on the record: Mr. Trump predicted a “very big” deal with Russia extending beyond Ukraine to “all of Europe,” in the Associated Press account filed below, and Mr. Barrot said he did not know what the American president had in mind. Russia has suggested there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says this time they will participate. Both statements stand. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side, and the talks have not begun.

The Gulf at 1800: Qeshm Again, Projectiles From Sirik, and a Gas Field Halted in Iraq

The strait’s file, which at midday stood at three claimed tanker fires and no names, added reports in both directions on Sunday evening and confirmed none of them. Late in the day, Al Jazeera Arabic cited Iran’s Tasnim agency as reporting that projectiles it attributed to the United States had come down on Qeshm Island, following an earlier report by the state agency IRNA of explosions on the island and sites possibly targeted; American involvement, any damage, and whether the impacts were separate from Saturday’s blasts all remain unverified, in the live file filed below. Iranian state television separately reported that three projectiles were launched from Sirik, on Iran’s southern coast, toward vessels it said were violating Iran’s navigation restrictions; whether any vessel was hit is not established. The Guards’ own statement of the morning, in the Guards’ outlet’s account filed below, holds the three tankers to have exploded and caught fire along an unauthorized route with their systems off, and attributes the burning to the “mischief” of the American army; the second account of the same statement, filed below, notes what the statement does not do—it does not say who caused the explosions and claims no strike by the Guards. No tanker has been named by any party at the evening hour, and the confirmed facts beside the claims stand where the midday edition left them: one rescue of 22 crew by the Emirates, one disabling of the M/V Huda explained by Central Command, neither joined by any authority to the Guards’ tally.

The evening’s one confirmed new fact in the region is in Iraq, and it is an interruption, not an explosion count. A drone attack on Sunday night halted production at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province, in Iraqi Kurdistan: the drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank and set it alight, two sources in the regional electricity ministry told Reuters; Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties; the Kurdistan Region’s electricity ministry said the interruption cut gas supplies to five power stations and estimated electricity generation would fall by 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts. No group had claimed responsibility at the evening hour. The land file moved in words at the same time: Mr. Trump said Task Force Iron Gate was operating at full capacity alongside the naval blockade, and the American Treasury has asked Baghdad to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran; Iraq’s foreign minister, Fuad Hussein, said Baghdad was still discussing the request and warned that widespread closures would hurt Iraq’s economy. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran’s two-day proposal remained on the table, calling on Washington to accept Iran’s conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts, and warning of retaliation if the United States resumed fighting. Mr. Trump, to CNN, supplied the other half of that exchange: fresh American strikes were “highly unlikely” if negotiations continued to advance, and the United States had identified 38 bridges as potential targets if military action resumed. No agreement has been announced by any party.

The Saudi–Yemen ledger also acquired its evening entries, each with its owner attached. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Yemen’s Saada region that it said were used in Sunday’s attack on Riyadh. The Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, claimed the movement had hit Riyadh’s financial district and targeted King Khalid International Airport; Saudi authorities did not confirm the airport was hit, and the Energy Ministry attributed the damage to the Aramco Tower to falling debris and reported no casualties there—against witness accounts, filed at midday, of broken glass on several floors and part of a facade torn away. The Houthis’ tally of coalition attacks in Yemen over the previous 24 hours stands at 91 in the evening’s live file and at 105, with six operations of their own claimed against Saudi sites, in the second account filed below; the two tallies are both the movement’s, taken at different hours, and neither has been verified. The Sanaa figure itself did not move: the Houthi-run health ministry’s count for Saturday’s strikes on homes near the capital stands at at least 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, with Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication saying it was investigating the report. Three officials told the Associated Press that Syria was preparing to send fighters to Saudi Arabia for a possible deployment along the Saudi side of the border with Yemen, an initial contingent of about 600 by one official’s account; a Syrian source had told state media on Saturday that Damascus had no plans to send troops into Yemen and described its cooperation with Riyadh as training and capacity-building. Both statements are in the file; neither has been acted on in any report taken in.

Jerusalem at 1800: Four Conditions, and the First Meetings Set

The mandate’s first evening produced conditions, not a coalition. After receiving the mandate at the 5 p.m. ceremony, Mr. Eisenkot said he would approach all Knesset factions and set four conditions for joining his government: accepting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, upholding the values of its Declaration of Independence, supporting universal military, national or civilian service, and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation, in the live file filed below. He challenged Likud and Religious Zionism—the parties of the prime minister he would replace and of the unity government Mr. Netanyahu proposed on Saturday—to back a government under his leadership if they stood by their calls for unity. No answer from either party was taken in by the evening. The week’s meetings are set: Mr. Eisenkot was expected to meet Naftali Bennett on Sunday evening and Avigdor Liberman on Monday. The Joint List told the broadcaster N12 it was willing to help end Mr. Netanyahu’s tenure without demanding a place in the government or the coalition, and that it had not yet been asked to commit to voting for an Eisenkot government. The arithmetic stands as the midday edition printed it: the four-party change bloc holds 48 of 120 seats, the Arab-led lists 19 between them, 61 are required, and the clock runs 28 days from today.

The argument that will decide the arithmetic was joined on Sunday, and it is the conscription argument. Mr. Liberman’s stated position, from Friday, is that he is prepared for “painful compromises”—including on the conscription law—to build a coalition of 61 without the Arab lists, and that he has not abandoned conscription, in the account of his announcement filed below. The assessment against it was filed Sunday afternoon: the commentator Amit Segal argued that the price of an arrangement among Liberman, Eisenkot, Bennett and the ultra-Orthodox parties was already established—the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted—in the afternoon file filed below. The other stated positions stand against any such price: the Democrats’ chairman, Yair Golan, wrote that a genuine partnership requires mutual responsibility and that the ultra-Orthodox must be drafted; the chief executive of Mr. Bennett’s party told its activists that silence does not imply consent, and restated the goal of a revolution in military service. The desk files the positions without choosing among them: a compromise offered, a price assessed, a draft demanded, and a silence that its owner says is not consent. The first test is Monday’s meeting.

Asunción at 1800: Twenty-Seven Charged, and $160 Million Paid Back

Paraguay’s file on its second day is a file of scale: the case’s width and the repayments’ width, printed side by side. At least 27 people face criminal charges in connection with the Ueno collapse, including the bank’s lead shareholder, Miguel Vazquez; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, in addition to the counts he shares with the former president; and each of Mr. Peña’s two charges—breach of trust and administration for personal gain—could carry a sentence of up to ten years, prosecutor Nancy Salomón said, in the evening account published at 15:39 ET and filed below. The sums are now in the record: Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including roughly $355 million in state pension funds, on the Reuters figures the account carries; the public and social-security funds it held in September 2026 are put at about 3.6 trillion guaraníes, with $163.8 million of the Itaipú hydroelectric dam’s funds among them, in the wire account and the evening brief filed below. The central bank began liquidation proceedings on November 2 after the bank’s solvency ratio fell to less than half the required minimum, and intervened the next day. On the other side of the ledger, the repayment has begun at scale: the central bank said $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, small depositors first, in sums up to 10 million guaraníes—about $1,600—with larger claims to be covered gradually, and banks opened weekend branches to serve customers. The state oil company Petropar has filed a complaint seeking protection for its assets. Mr. Peña declined to testify at Saturday’s hearing; his lawyer, Ricardo Preda, maintains the plea of not guilty and his own forecast of the case: “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” The opposition’s stated position is Senator Yolanda Paredes’s: the former president “must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison.” He remains, on the judge’s order, at the Presidential Escort Regiment. President Pedro Alliana is naming a new cabinet to serve through 2028. The charges are charges; no court has ruled on any part of the case, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them.

Washington at 1800: The Handover Comes Monday, and the Responses Are In

The White House change announced on Friday takes effect on Monday, and Sunday was the day the considered responses were filed. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and the president’s homeland security adviser, becomes chief of staff on November 9; Susie Wiles, who gave the president her resignation on Thursday night and whose last day in the post was Friday, moves to the Trump Political Operation, in the account of the announcement filed below. The president’s words on his choice are in the record: “Stephen’s been with me since the beginning. He gets it,” and, departing the White House on Friday, “Stephen’s been great, and sometimes in life, you gotta make moves.” The Senate Democratic leader’s answer supplies the opposition’s reading in one sentence, as the account’s headline carries it: Senator Chuck Schumer’s verdict is that Mr. Trump “has learned nothing from his historic defeat.” From inside the president’s own party, Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, whose vote share fell from 65 percent in 2024 to under 55 this year, called the promotion a mistake: “If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” in the evening brief filed below. The reading from Paris, filed Friday, is that the appointment is a doubling down—a retreat into the inner circle after a majority of voters punished the president’s choices at the midterms. The desk files the four readings without adopting one: the president’s loyalty, the opposition’s verdict, a congressman’s dissent from his own side, and an ally-capital’s interpretation. What is not in dispute is the sequence—a resignation offered Thursday night, an announcement Friday, a handover Monday. The Federal Register published nothing on November 7 or November 8, in the Sunday situation report filed below; the weekend’s Washington record is personnel and statements, and the desk files it as such.

The Count at 1800: Frozen at Friday’s Figures, the Estimates Widen

Neither Senate race moved on Sunday, and the correction this watch owes is that nothing has moved since Friday evening. Mississippi’s tally stands where it stood at midday: Scott Colom, the Democrat, at 467,930 votes to the incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 465,356—a margin of 2,574 on 953,314 counted, 97 percent of the estimated total—and the Sunday situation report, filed below, dates that tally precisely: it is stamped 5:02 p.m. on Friday, November 6, and the results page updated at 3:16 a.m. ET on Sunday shows the same two totals, so no votes have been posted since Friday evening. What moved on Sunday is the estimate of what remains, and the estimates do not agree: the state Republican chairman, Mike Hurst, told CNN that between 23,000 and 25,000 affidavit or mail-in ballots were outstanding, a wider figure than the 10,000 to 15,000 provisional ballots carried on Saturday and wider than the roughly 3,139 mail ballots the Sunday video roundup counts as outstanding. The desk prints the three figures with their owners and chooses in none of them; the calendar is the settled part—mailed ballots must be received, and affidavit voters must cure a missing identification, by 5 p.m. on Tuesday, November 10, counties certify by November 13, Mississippi law provides no recount for this race, and a plurality wins. Alaska stands at 637 first-choice votes, Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan at 48.2 percent to 47.9 with about 74 percent counted; the next count is expected Monday or Tuesday, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no candidate clears 50 percent. The ledgers above the two races stand at 252 Democrats to 161 Republicans in the House, with 22 House races uncalled, and 54 to 44 in the Senate, in the Associated Press ledger the Sunday report reads. The prediction market’s prices, printed as the venue’s and not the desk’s, put Mr. Colom at 99.0 percent and Ms. Peltola at 98.6—a forecast standing beside a frozen count. At 1800 on the fifth day after the election, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1800: The Count of the Hurt Settles at 22

Central Japan’s correction file, which at midday ran from 15 to 24 injured, settled in the afternoon reports. The afternoon official reports list 19 injured in Aichi Prefecture—one serious injury and 18 minor—and three minor injuries in Shizuoka, 22 in all, in the afternoon account filed below; the television count carried in the second file below gives the same division, 19 in Aichi including one serious case and three in Shizuoka, where an 80-year-old woman fell in Hamamatsu’s Hamana Ward. The morning’s lower figure, 15, was the count of an assessment in its first hours; the 24 carried by some accounts remains in the record as the highest figure printed, and the afternoon official division is the one the desk carries forward. The earthquake itself stands as filed: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka at about 40 kilometres’ depth, upper 5 on the Japanese scale in Chita, Aichi, no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The agency’s Sunday acts are also in the file: having regard to loosened ground, it lowered the thresholds for issuing landslide warnings for the municipalities of Aichi that shook hardest, and its standing guidance—caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that this quake’s pattern is unlikely to lead to the Nankai Trough megaquake—stands unrevised. A second, separate tremor, magnitude 4.3 in the Kumamoto area at 10:53 a.m., produced no reports of serious damage or injury. Particulars of the hurt are in the accounts: in Tokoname a woman in her fifties was taken to hospital with a fractured ankle; in Toyota a man in his forties and a woman in her eighties fell and struck their heads and were conscious in hospital. The sleeper train Sunrise Izumo made a temporary stop; none of its approximately 290 passengers was reported hurt.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Board, and a Monday That Must Reprice the Weekend

There was no American or European session on Sunday, so the desk prints the board the weekend leaves and the questions Monday must answer. Friday’s close stands as the Sunday situation report carries it: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.31 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.425, up 1.09 percent; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; and the VIX at 25.64, down 9.01 percent. The ten-year Treasury yielded 4.859 percent; gold’s last print was $4,079.50. Oil’s settlements stand where the midday edition printed them—Brent at $98.32 a barrel, West Texas Intermediate at $90.83—on a week that took about 13 percent off the barrel on the desk’s baseline and about 17 percent on the Sunday newsletter’s, the disagreement filed at midday and unrevised here. The one Sunday session in the file, India’s seventy-minute Diwali Muhurat sitting, closed up 400 points on the Sensex. What Monday holds is a list, not a forecast: the first full session since three tanker fires were claimed in the strait and a drone halted a gas field that feeds five power stations; a chief of staff taking office in Washington; coalition meetings in Jerusalem; and, on Tuesday, the Abu Dhabi talks and the counting deadlines in two American states. The steepest Friday move in the file is Tokyo’s: the Nikkei 225 fell 5.96 percent on Friday, the evening brief notes. Monday’s open is the first price the weekend’s claims will meet.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Al-Ayyat, the dead agree at seven in every later account and the injured stand at 112 in the ministry’s later count and 125 in another account of the ministry’s figures; the desk carries the seven and prints both injured figures. On Kraków, the wounded stand at 15 or 16 by the hour and the source; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief, at 53, 52 and 21 in the police statement, and the sister at 20 in the prosecutors’; the joining of the two crime scenes stands at a spokesman’s “highly likely”; and the minister’s reading stands as a hypothesis its author declines to withdraw and its critics demand he document. On Hormuz, three tanker fires are claimed by the force that polices the route, one projectile report on Qeshm is attributed by one agency to the United States and confirmed by no one, three projectiles from Sirik are reported by a state broadcaster with no hit established, and the one confirmed interruption of the evening is a gas field in Iraq stopped by a drone nobody has claimed. On Riyadh, the damage is debris in the ministry’s account and torn facade in the witnesses’, and the Houthis’ own tally of the coalition’s attacks stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. On the count, the margins are Friday’s and the outstanding-ballot estimates run from about three thousand to twenty-five thousand depending on who is counting what. On Shizuoka, the hurt settled at 22 in the afternoon official division, between a morning 15 and a printed 24. On Jerusalem, a mandate has been exercised in words—four conditions, published on its first evening—and no government exists. On Asunción, the detention is a fact, the charges are allegations carrying stated penalties, the repayments are a central bank’s figures, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at 1800 with everything of consequence in this file falling on the same two days: Monday’s handovers and meetings, and Tuesday’s talks and deadlines.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-eight items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting as security fears growKRAKOW, Nov 8: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in the southern city’s historic main square, an attack the government said was likely inspired by far-right ideology, following a string of October school stabbings officials linked to extremist content online. Sixteen people were wounded in addition to those killed, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital. One of the dead was a British citizen and another Austrian; five foreign nationals, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that the three bodies at the home had gunshot wounds, with firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition recovered from the property. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s Saturday reading drew a demand from PiS deputy head Przemysław Czarnek for explanations and the information behind it; on Sunday the minister told TVN24 he was not retracting his statements and that the motive investigation was ongoing. The square and surrounding streets reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s was suspended for twelve hours, the first time since 1939, PAP reported; police tightened security in Warsaw and other cities; and the two wounded officers have regained consciousness.

 SubjectivePollar — Evening Brief, 8 November: Kraków mourns, Miller prepares, trains collide, Peña detainedThe evening brief, compiled from Der Tagesspiegel, TVP Info, Polsat News, ANSA and others: officials counted Kraków’s six dead as a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50; reports put the wounded at 15 or 16; prosecutors said the two wounded officers had been woken from drug-induced comas after surgery while the suspect remained critical under guard; police found his 52-year-old father, 51-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister shot dead in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; and Italian students who sheltered in a cafe left by bus for Italy. On Washington: Donald Trump named Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff from November 9, and Representative Marlin Stutzman called the promotion a mistake. On Egypt: a Giza-to-Fayoum train ran into the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan train at Al-Ayyat; the toll rose through the afternoon from 64 injured and no confirmed deaths to at least seven dead and 112 injured, with 52 to 72 ambulances reported and President al-Sisi ordering an investigation. On Paraguay: prosecutors say Ueno Bank held about 3.6 trillion guaraníes in public and social-security funds in September 2026, including $163.8 million of Itaipú funds; by November 8 the central bank said 1.2 million customers had received partial or full reimbursement, small depositors first up to 10 million guaraníes; Petropar filed a complaint; and President Alliana began naming a new cabinet.

 SubjectiveAAP — Poland in mourning after the Kraków mass shootingPoland has begun two days of national mourning after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into the busy central square in Kraków and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him; the defence minister described the attack as an “act of terror.” By Saturday evening mourners had left candles, the square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as the investigation continued, and St Mary’s Trumpet Call was paused overnight in tribute.  SubjectiveHong Kong Business Wire, carrying AFP — impeached Paraguay leader charged over the bank implosionParaguayan prosecutors charged ex-president Santiago Peña and took him into custody on Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests. Peña, Paraguay’s youngest-ever president, was removed by the Senate on Friday, three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links, and was brought before prosecutors and charged with “breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain” after about three hours of questioning over his links to Ueno Bank, a digital-first company with which nearly half of Paraguay’s population of 6.5 million have accounts. An indictment states that “between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities” and “was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank’s economic group in an irregular manner.” Peña spent Friday night in custody after being arrested within an hour of his impeachment trial; protesters gathered outside his home to demand he be locked up in a regular prison. He was replaced by former vice president Pedro Alliana, who promised not to abandon the almost three million depositors, including pensioners, affected by Ueno’s demise; thousands had taken to the streets demanding their money back after the central bank took control of Ueno, citing fears for its solvency.
